title: How do Organisms Reproduce?
subject: science
syllabus_note: Follows the CBSE 2025-26 syllabus: reproduction in animals and plants (asexual and sexual), reproductive health, need for and methods of family planning, safe sex vs HIV/AIDS, childbearing and women's health.

blocks.title: Same, but not quite the same
blocks.body:
Puppies look like dogs, mango seeds grow into mango trees, and you look like your parents. Yet no two puppies, or two mango trees, or two brothers, are exactly alike.

Reproduction makes new individuals that are **similar** to their parents, but not identical. In this chapter you will see why this small difference matters, how single cells, plants and humans reproduce, and how people can take care of their reproductive health.

blocks.title: Fertilisation in a test tube
blocks.body:
Panchanan Maheshwari, born in Jaipur, was one of the world's leading experts on how flowering plants form embryos. His book on the **embryology of flowering plants** (1950) became a standard text.

At the University of Delhi, his group grew flower parts in test tubes and achieved **fertilisation in a test tube**, opening the way to new methods of plant breeding. He was elected a Fellow of the Royal Society in 1965.
blocks.future: Reproductive biology leads to careers in medicine and nursing, plant breeding and seed science, animal husbandry, tissue culture and biotechnology.

blocks.question: If DNA were copied perfectly every time, what would all the offspring of an asexual organism be like?
options: Exactly identical to the parent and to each other
blocks.explanation: Variation comes from small errors in DNA copying; with perfect copying there would be no variation at all.

blocks.title: Copies with small changes
blocks.body:
The **DNA** in the nucleus carries the information for making proteins, and so for the body design. The basic event in reproduction is making a **copy of the DNA**, along with extra cell apparatus, so that two cells form.

- The copying is very accurate but never perfect, so the copies are similar but have small **variations**.
- Consistency in DNA copying keeps the body design that suits the organism's **niche** (its place in the environment).
- Variation is useful for the **species**, not necessarily for the individual. If the niche changes drastically, for example the water gets hotter, most bacteria may die, but a few variants that resist heat survive and grow. Variation is therefore the basis for **evolution**.

blocks.question: Why is variation useful for a species?
options: Some variants may survive if the environment changes
blocks.explanation: When conditions change, some variants may be suited to the new conditions, so the species survives.
option_feedback: A variation may not help the individual at all.

blocks.title: One parent
blocks.body:
In **asexual reproduction** a single parent produces offspring, with no gametes. The offspring are almost identical to the parent.

- **Fission:** unicellular organisms split. Amoeba can split in any plane; **Leishmania** (which causes kala-azar) has a whip-like structure at one end and splits in a definite plane. The malaria parasite **Plasmodium** divides into many daughter cells at once (multiple fission).
- **Fragmentation:** simple multicellular organisms such as **Spirogyra** break into pieces that grow into new individuals.
- **Regeneration:** **Hydra** and **Planaria** can be cut into pieces, and each piece grows into a complete organism, using specialised cells that divide and develop into different tissues. Complex organisms cannot do this, because their cells are highly specialised.
- **Budding:** in **Hydra** a bud develops as an outgrowth and detaches when mature.
- **Vegetative propagation:** new plants grow from roots, stems or leaves (layering, grafting). Buds in the notches of **Bryophyllum** leaves grow into new plants. It is used for plants that have lost the ability to produce seeds (banana, orange, rose, jasmine); the plants are genetically similar to the parent and bear flowers and fruits earlier. **Tissue culture** grows many plants from a few cells.
- **Spore formation:** bread mould (**Rhizopus**) forms spores in sporangia. Spores have thick walls that protect them until they reach a moist surface.

blocks.title: Methods of asexual reproduction
blocks.body:
| Method | How it happens | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Binary fission | one cell splits into two | Amoeba, Leishmania |
| Multiple fission | one cell divides into many daughter cells | Plasmodium |
| Fragmentation | the body breaks into pieces; each grows into a new individual | Spirogyra |
| Regeneration | a cut piece grows into a complete organism, using specialised cells | Hydra, Planaria |
| Budding | an outgrowth (bud) grows and separates | Hydra, yeast |
| Vegetative propagation | a new plant grows from a root, stem or leaf | sugarcane, rose, grapes, Bryophyllum |
| Spore formation | spores in sporangia grow on a moist surface | Rhizopus (bread mould) |

blocks.question: Which organism reproduces by multiple fission?
blocks.explanation: The malaria parasite Plasmodium divides into many daughter cells at once.

blocks.title: Flowers, pollination and fertilisation
blocks.body:
In **sexual reproduction**, two **germ cells (gametes)**, one from each parent, fuse. Each gamete has **half** the usual number of chromosomes and half the DNA, so the zygote has the full amount again. Combining DNA from two individuals produces more variation. The male gamete is usually small and motile; the female gamete is larger and stores food.

**Parts of a flower:** sepals, petals, **stamens** (male; the anther makes pollen grains) and **pistil** (female; ovary, style and stigma). The ovary contains **ovules**, each with an egg cell. A flower with only stamens or only a pistil is **unisexual** (papaya, watermelon); one with both is **bisexual** (Hibiscus, mustard).

- **Pollination:** transfer of pollen from the anther to the stigma: of the same flower (**self-pollination**) or of another flower (**cross-pollination**, by wind, water or animals).
- **Fertilisation:** a **pollen tube** grows from the pollen grain through the style to the ovule, and the male germ cell fuses with the egg to form a **zygote**.
- **After fertilisation:** the zygote divides to form the **embryo**; the ovule develops a tough coat and becomes the **seed**; the ovary grows and ripens into the **fruit**; petals, sepals, stamens, style and stigma may shrivel and fall off.
- The seed contains the future plant, which grows into a seedling under the right conditions (**germination**).

blocks.question: After fertilisation, the ovary develops into the:
blocks.explanation: The ovule becomes the seed and the ovary ripens into the fruit.
option_feedback: The pollen tube grows from the pollen grain.

blocks.title: Puberty and the reproductive systems
blocks.body:
**Puberty** is the period when the reproductive tissues begin to mature.
- Common changes: thick hair in the armpits and genital area; thinner hair on the legs, arms and face; oily skin and pimples.
- In girls: breasts begin to grow and the skin of the nipples darkens; **menstruation** starts.
- In boys: hair on the face, the voice begins to crack, and the penis occasionally becomes enlarged and erect.

**Male reproductive system:** the **testes**, in the scrotum outside the abdomen (because sperm formation needs a lower temperature), produce **sperms** and the hormone **testosterone**. Sperms travel through the **vas deferens**, which joins a tube from the urinary bladder; the **urethra** is a common passage for sperms and urine. The **seminal vesicles** and **prostate gland** add secretions, so the sperms are in a fluid that makes their transport easier and gives them nutrition.

**Female reproductive system:** the **ovaries** release one egg every month and make the hormones oestrogen and progesterone. The egg travels through the **oviduct (fallopian tube)** to the **uterus**, which opens into the vagina through the cervix. Fertilisation happens in the oviduct. The zygote is implanted in the thick lining of the uterus.

**Placenta:** a disc-like tissue embedded in the uterine wall. Villi on the embryo's side face blood spaces on the mother's side, giving a large surface for **glucose and oxygen** to pass to the embryo and **wastes** to pass to the mother. The child develops in about nine months.

**Menstruation:** every month the uterus prepares a thick, spongy lining with blood vessels. If the egg is not fertilised, this lining slowly breaks down and comes out through the vagina as blood and mucus. This cycle takes place roughly every month and usually lasts about two to eight days.

blocks.question: Where does fertilisation take place in the human female?
blocks.explanation: The sperm meets the egg in the oviduct; the zygote then moves to the uterus and is implanted.
option_feedback: The zygote is implanted in the uterus after fertilisation.

blocks.title: Health, contraception and the sex ratio
blocks.body:
Reproductive health means physical and emotional well-being related to reproduction, including the right age and readiness for having children.

**Sexually transmitted diseases (STDs)** spread through sexual contact: bacterial, such as **gonorrhoea** and **syphilis**; viral, such as **warts** and **HIV-AIDS**. A condom helps to prevent many of them.

**Contraception** prevents pregnancy:

| Method | How it works |
|---|---|
| Mechanical barrier | condoms or similar coverings stop the sperm from reaching the egg; also protect against many infections |
| Hormonal | oral pills change the hormonal balance so that eggs are not released |
| Copper-T or loop | placed in the uterus to prevent pregnancy |
| Surgical | vas deferens blocked in males, or fallopian tube blocked in females |

**Sex ratio:** prenatal sex determination is prohibited by law in India. Selective killing of female foetuses (**female foeticide**) is a crime, and it is reducing the number of girls in some parts of the country. A healthy society needs a healthy sex ratio.

blocks.question: Which contraceptive method also protects against many sexually transmitted diseases?
blocks.explanation: A condom is a mechanical barrier, so it also stops the spread of many infections; the others do not.

blocks.title: Ovule to seed, ovary to fruit
blocks.body:
- **Ovul-e → s-e-ed** (both have an 'e' sound); **ovar-y → fruit-y** (the bigger part becomes the bigger thing).
- **Asexual methods, in order of the chapter:** **F**ission, **F**ragmentation, **R**egeneration, **B**udding, **V**egetative propagation, **S**pores: "**F**ive **F**riends **R**ode **B**ikes **V**ery **S**lowly".
- **Sperm path:** testis → vas deferens → urethra (with seminal vesicles and prostate adding fluid).

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.body:
- Writing that pollination and fertilisation are the same: pollination moves pollen; fertilisation is the fusion of gametes.
- Writing that the ovary becomes the seed: the ovule becomes the seed; the ovary becomes the fruit.
- Saying that Amoeba reproduces by budding: Amoeba uses binary fission; Hydra and yeast use budding.
- Writing that copper-T protects against STDs: only barrier methods such as condoms do.
- Writing that the testes are inside the abdomen: they are in the scrotum, outside, because they need a lower temperature.

blocks.title: Show it in class
blocks.body: Cut a Hibiscus or mustard flower lengthwise and let students find the sepals, petals, anthers, stigma, style and ovary with a hand lens. Grow bread mould on moist bread for Rhizopus, and put a Bryophyllum leaf on moist soil to show buds growing from its edges. Handle the human reproduction topic factually and respectfully, and let students ask questions in writing if they are shy.

blocks.title: Explain it in your own words
blocks.body: Explain to a friend why bananas are grown from suckers and not seeds, and why sexual reproduction gives more variation than asexual reproduction.

blocks.title: Where this leads
blocks.body:
- **Chapter 6:** testosterone and oestrogen bring the changes of puberty.
- **Chapter 8, Heredity:** how traits pass from parents to offspring through DNA.
- **Class 12 Biology:** reproduction in flowering plants, human reproduction and reproductive health in detail.

blocks.title: Mastery challenge
blocks.body:
A farmer has a mango tree that gives very sweet fruit. He wants many trees with exactly the same fruit.

(a) Should he grow them from seeds? (b) What method should he use? (c) Give one advantage and one disadvantage of this method.

**Answer:** (a) No: seeds come from sexual reproduction, so the new trees would show variation and the fruit may not be as sweet. (b) Vegetative propagation, for example grafting. (c) Advantage: the new plants are genetically similar to the parent and bear fruit earlier. Disadvantage: there is no variation, so all the trees may be harmed alike by a new disease.

blocks.title: Chapter summary
blocks.body:
- Reproduction involves copying DNA; small copying errors cause variation, which helps a species survive changes and is the basis of evolution.
- Asexual reproduction: fission, fragmentation, regeneration, budding, vegetative propagation and spore formation.
- Sexual reproduction combines DNA from two parents through gametes with half the chromosomes, giving more variation.
- In flowering plants, pollination is followed by fertilisation; the ovule becomes the seed and the ovary the fruit.
- In humans, puberty prepares the body; testes make sperms, ovaries release eggs; the embryo is nourished through the placenta; menstruation occurs when the egg is not fertilised.
- Contraceptive methods and awareness of STDs protect reproductive health; female foeticide is illegal.

blocks.title: Board exam tips
blocks.body:
- Practise labelled diagrams: longitudinal section of a flower, germination of pollen on the stigma, binary fission in Amoeba, budding in Hydra, and the human male and female reproductive systems.
- Learn one example for each asexual method.
- Know the three changes in a flower after fertilisation (SQP marking scheme).
- In 'difference' questions (pollination vs fertilisation, asexual vs sexual, binary vs multiple fission), write points in a table.

blocks.front: What does the ovule become after fertilisation?
blocks.back: The seed (the ovary becomes the fruit).
Passes glucose and oxygen from the mother to the embryo, and wastes from the embryo to the mother.

blocks.front: Why are the testes outside the abdomen?
blocks.back: Sperm formation needs a temperature lower than the normal body temperature.
